extracted.intended_audience: NaNoWriMo participants and aspiring novelists / creative writers attempting a month-long draft
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical/psychological guidelines for drafting a novel during National Novel Writing Month (50,000 words in 30 days). Focuses on time management, mindset, drafting strategies, and self-care to survive and finish the month.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet the NaNoWriMo 50,000-word goal
rubrics_metrics.description: NaNoWriMo is a month-long event that challenges people to write 50,000 words in 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official site resources, sponsor discounts, forums for brainstorming and advice, and Twitter sprints to help reach the daily/total wordcount. The 50,000 target is the formal goal of the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome the blank page — just write
rubrics_metrics.description: "The blank page is yours. Cast aside worries over art and criticism... Forget those voices." — Chuck Wendig
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let fear of art/criticism or perfectionism paralyze you; write something, anything, to get started. The emphasis is on producing words rather than waiting for perfect inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept imperfect first drafts and expect change
rubrics_metrics.description: "You have to accept that your story will change as you write it... The moment you try to put things into words is when you find all the problems." — Andy Weir
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the gap between the story in your head and what appears on the page; early 'stupid' or flawed passages are normal and part of the revision process. Treat the draft as phase one of making the story better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave room for surprises — be flexible even if you outline
rubrics_metrics.description: "Even if you’re an outliner, leave room for the unexpected things to sneak in... Surprises are half the fun... you can always edit them out after November." — Erin Morgenstern
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow spontaneity and unplanned tangents or subplots during the draft; they can produce important material or be removed later. Balance planning with openness to the story evolving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make time — schedule writing into your life
rubrics_metrics.description: "Try writing on your lunch hour. Try getting up a few hours early each day... Experiment. The goal is to show yourself that you can make room for writing in your life." — Brandon Sanderson
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as time that must be deliberately found; experiment with short windows (lunch, early morning) and eliminate distractions (TV, games). Finding sustainable routines now helps if you intend to write professionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set daily/scene-level goals to maintain momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: "Perhaps you might want to try setting a new goal a day. Go over what must happen in each day’s pages to move you along until tomorrow." — Charlaine Harris
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the month into manageable daily objectives or scene targets to push the story forward, especially to survive the 'middle' where many projects stall. If you lack specifics, stay open to surprises but aim for movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist through hard writing days — prioritize output
rubrics_metrics.description: "No one can tell if the writing was fun or if it was hard... Get the words down anyway." — Holly Black
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some writing sessions will be slow or miserable; continue producing words rather than waiting for effortless inspiration. The quality of the process is less visible than the fact of having produced pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on writing, not publishing or business concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: "Forget about all that [publishing/business] when you’re actually writing... being published is not a necessary validation." — Garth Nix
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defer worries about agents, marketing, and the business side until after you have a finished novel. Write for the work itself—many participants are not aiming for publication and finishing is valuable on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and manage self-doubt — don't be overwhelmed
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is what makes you a writer... the utter conviction that you are the Worst and your novel is the Worst... But writers do not let this feeling overwhelm them." — N.K. Jemisin
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-doubt is normal, even for successful authors; acknowledge it but keep writing. Emotional turbulence does not invalidate the work-in-progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize self-care and balance to sustain productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Position yourself to succeed by doing the other things in your life that rejuvenate you... Some form of exercise... eating chocolate, or taking time off to watch part of a TV show." — Jeff VanderMeer
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid burning out by maintaining physical and mental health: exercise, small rewards, breaks, and recreation. Exhaustion reduces both writing quality and ability to meet goals—balance increases endurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgive missed days and value incremental progress
rubrics_metrics.description: "Writing begins with forgiveness. Let go of the shame about how long it’s been since you last wrote... Even if you don't reach 50,000 words, that's still more than what you started with on November 1." — Daniel José Older
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat missed sessions or falling short of the 50k target as part of the process; celebrate increases in output even if the official goal isn't met. Self-forgiveness sustains long-term writing habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish the draft first; editing comes later
rubrics_metrics.description: "Writing the draft is an act of faith... once you have something, you can make it better. The only thing you can’t fix is a blank page." — V.E. Schwab
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize completing the manuscript during NaNoWriMo and postpone intensive editing until after you have a full draft. The imperative is to produce material to revise, since you can't revise what doesn't exist.
